title: Private security firms will soon be allowed to hack overseas cybercriminals
gist: A Trump National Security Presidential Memorandum directs the National Coordination Center to build a program letting vetted private security firms conduct offensive cyber surveillance and effects operations against foreign transnational criminal organizations — the first time Washington has authorized private offensive hacking — with $1 million escrow deposits required and implementation details due from DOJ and DHS within 60 days.

themes.theme: A first-of-its-kind privatization of offensive cyber

insights.claim: A National Security Presidential Memorandum issued Thursday directs the National Coordination Center, operating under the Homeland Security Task Force, to develop a program of cyber operations against foreign transnational criminal organizations with Justice and Homeland Security providing oversight.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A new federal program category creates a direct contracting channel for offensive-capable security firms — a revenue line that did not legally exist before.
insights.locator: The Trump administration is recruiting private security firms

insights.claim: This is the first time the US federal government will authorize private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against overseas hackers; until now the government prohibited private-sector action of this kind without court-authorized approval.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A structural legal shift, not an incremental policy tweak — it opens a new market and a new liability regime simultaneously.
insights.quote: The new program is the first time the federal government will authorize private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against overseas hackers.
insights.locator: The new program is the first time

insights.claim: The memo appears to permit participating companies to use spyware or launch offensive attacks intended to destroy TCO data or systems, and does not rule out attacks using encryption to lock targets out of their networks or distributed denial-of-service attacks.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Sanctioning the use of ransomware-style and DDoS techniques by private actors is a normative shift with escalation and attribution implications.
insights.locator: The memo appears to permit companies participating

insights.claim: The accompanying fact sheet lists ransomware, sextortion schemes, phishing campaigns, financial fraud and impersonation scams as the criminal activities eligible for private-sector targeting.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The eligible-target list defines the addressable scope for firms building offensive practices — ransomware operators are the primary market.
insights.locator: Devil will be in the still-undefined details

themes.theme: Scope limits and the state-actor carve-out

insights.claim: Eligible targets are defined as any foreign group conducting cyber-enabled crime against the US government, US persons or US interests that is not an institutional part of a foreign government or wholly operated under a foreign government's direction — explicitly excluding state-run hacking operations.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The state-actor exclusion is the key boundary; given how blurred criminal and state-directed hacking has become, attribution disputes will determine the program's real scope.
insights.quote: not an institutional part of a foreign government or wholly operated under a foreign government’s direction

insights.claim: Cyber Effects and Cyber Surveillance Operations under the program may not produce 'Critical Outcomes' — defined as loss of life, serious injury, or actions rising to the level of use of force or armed attack under international law.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The international-law threshold is the escalation firewall; how DOJ and DHS operationalize it in 60 days determines the program's real risk profile.
insights.locator: The memo placed specific limits on the scope

insights.claim: Participating companies must be vetted and approved by the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security against minimum standards covering technical proficiency, proven cyber operations performance, facility security, personnel vetting, competence and reliability.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Facility-security and personnel-vetting requirements favor incumbents with existing clearances — a barrier that concentrates the opportunity among a handful of firms.
insights.locator: Private companies must first be approved after vetting

insights.claim: Participating companies must deposit $1 million in escrow, forfeited if the company falls into non-compliance with its contractual agreement under the program.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A $1 million forfeitable bond is small relative to program risk but large enough to screen out small firms — expect a concentrated participant list.
insights.locator: Participating companies must also deposit $1 million

insights.claim: Independent security researcher Kevin Beamont concedes there is merit in hacking ransomware groups and says it already happens in practice, but insists the correct incentives must be in place for a formal program to work.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Practitioner acknowledgment that offensive counter-ransomware already occurs informally means the memo legalizes existing practice more than it creates new capability.
insights.quote: There’s definitely merit in the idea of hacking ransomware groups and it does already in fact happen (don’t ask me how I know)
insights.locator: There's definitely merit in the idea

insights.claim: Beamont argues the biggest obstacle to fighting ransomware over the past five years has been private cyber companies lobbying for nothing to change because they profit from the status quo, making it optimistic to put those same firms in charge of stopping it.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The core structural critique: vendors monetizing ransomware defense have negative incentive to eliminate ransomware — a conflict the program does not address.
insights.quote: A lot of companies have made a lot of money, so putting them in charge of stopping it seems optimistic.
insights.locator: The biggest problem I've had with fighting ransomware

themes.theme: Implementation risk in the undefined details

insights.claim: Many specifics of the policy remain undefined and the memo gives Justice and Homeland Security 60 days to deliver them, meaning the program's effectiveness and judiciousness are not yet determinable.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A dated 60-day deliverable is the concrete catalyst to watch — the implementing guidance will reveal which firms and capabilities actually qualify.
insights.quote: The memo directs the Justice and Homeland Security departments to deliver the particulars in the next 60 days.
insights.locator: Many of the specifics of the policy remain undefined

insights.claim: The lynchpin of the program is bringing private sector companies in to participate, meaning the government is structurally dependent on commercial capability rather than expanding its own offensive cyber workforce.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Government dependence on commercial offensive capability strengthens the negotiating position of firms that hold it — pricing power in an emerging category.
insights.quote: The lynchpin of that program is bringing in private sector companies to participate.
insights.locator: The Departments of Justice and Homeland Security will provide oversight
